title: Psychometrics Portfolio
text:
Introduction
This portfolio is my attempt to catalog and showcase the various kinds of analyses that a psychometrician might perform with different kinds of data in different fields. The portfolio is structured as a series of projects; each involves taking a particular real-world dataset and running a comprehensive set of analyses which are appropriate for the properties of the data and the goals of stakeholders. All analyses are performed using the R programming language and the RStudio integrated development environment (IDE).
This portfolio is also intended to be an open educational resource (OER) and can be used by anyone who wants to learn how to conduct psychometric analyses in R. This portfolio is far from ideal for self-study; it is neither highly self-contained nor highly expository, as would be expected in a textbook. Rather, I sprinkle in various theoretical comments and proofs where I feel that they are illustrative. Nevertheless, I hope that whoever reads this portfolio can find some value in the project/case study structure.
The inspiration for this portfolio stems from my observation that, while there are a large number of excellent resources on the theory of psychometrics and applications in R, there are few resources that capture what the actual work of a psychometrician might look like in the form of projects. In my own learning, I have found that it is easy to get lost in theory without a clear sense of direction or indication as to whether one is actually learning. Furthermore, it can be very daunting to learn sophisticated methods and to keep track of what one has seen and understood. Creating this portfolio has been helpful for me in these respects. Another inspiration for this portfolio is the book “Psychometrics in Exercises using R and RStudio” by Anna Brown, which I found to be especially helpful in my learning, and which shares many of the same design principles as this portfolio.

title: Psychometrics Portfolio
text:
Reproducibility
This portfolio was designed with reproducibility in mind. Reproducibility asks the following question: given the same dataset analyzed using the same methods, can an independent researcher obtain the same results at a later time? Reproducibility is often confused with replicability, which asks a different question: given a new dataset collected and analyzed using the same methods, can an independent researcher obtain similar results? Replicability is often more scientifically interesting, but it is of theoretical rather than pragmatic concern; a replication failure may undermine a potential scientific theory. Reproducibility, on the other hand, is an essential practice for reporting and making decisions based on the results of analyses; a reproducibility failure undermines the transparency and trustworthiness of the results.
For those who simply wish to follow along with the analyses in this portfolio, the reproducibility elements included are likely unnecessary. Simply load the required packages and run the code. In most cases, the exact same results should appear.
For those who wish to reproduce the analyses almost exactly, this portfolio utilizes the {renv} package (Ushey & Wickham, 2026), which creates reproducible environments for R projects. {renv} works by creating a project library that contains only the packages used in this portfolio. Additionally, {renv} creates a lockfile that contains the specific versions of every package used, as well as the repositories where the package versions are stored. The Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) is the most popular repository; however, CRAN only stores the latest versions of packages. Instead, the {renv} packages uses the Posit Public Package Manager (P3M), as it stores older package versions. P3M has an additional benefit for reproducibility, which is that it stores daily snapshots of CRAN; this means that an independent researcher can load the exact same package versions that were used by the author of the analyses on the day that the analyses were originally performed.
To reproduce the analyses, I first recommend using a tool such as rig (an R installation manager which allows for switching between multiple versions of R) to load the exact R version recorded in the renv.lock file. This is because {renv} may run into issues if a different version of R is used. To avoid headaches, it is easier to load the exact R version recorded using rig.
Next, the following steps can be used to reproduce the portfolio:

Make sure that RStudio and rig are installed.
Clone the github repository for the portfolio website by running git clone https://github.com/wyck-psych/wyck-psych.github.io.git in the terminal.
Change the directory to the cloned project folder by typing cd followed by a space in the terminal and then dragging the cloned project folder into the terminal window. Most terminals will auto-fill the correct path to the project folder. Typically on Windows, the cloned project folder ends up in your \Users folder. Then run the full command, which will look something like cd C:\Users\winso\wyck-psych.github.io.
Once the directory is set to the cloned project folder, run rig rstudio renv.lock in the terminal. This tells rig to open RStudio using the R version recorded in the renv.lock file. If that R version is not currently installed, rig will prompt you to install it.
Once the project is opened in RStudio, run renv::restore() in the R console. This will install the exact date-snapshotted package versions into the project library.
Once the packages are restored, the entire portfolio can be reproduced by running quarto render in RStudio’s built-in terminal (Tools → Terminal).

title: Project 1 - Foundational Analyses using Multiple-Choice Response Data from an Achievement Test
text:
1.0) Introduction
In this project, we will be analyzing the Homeostasis Concept Inventory (HCI) (McFarland et al. 2017), which is a 20-item multiple-choice test designed to measure undergraduate students’ understanding of the homeostasis concept in physiology. The HCI was developed through an iterative process which involved identifying common student misconceptions through think-aloud interviews and expert feedback. Distractors were then developed based on these misconceptions.
The dataset HCIdata is part of the {ShinyItemAnalysis} R package (Martinková and Hladká 2023) and contains N=669 observations which were collected as part of the validation process for the final version of the HCI. Notably, the dataset contains the unscored item responses, which allows for distractor analysis, as well as matching variables such as gender and minority membership, which allows for differential item functioning (DIF) analyses.
The HCIdata dataset contains 49 variables. The first 20 variables (1-20) are the unscored item responses, which are recorded as capital letters (e.g. “A”, “B”, “C”). The next 20 variables (21-40) are the scored item responses which are recorded as “0” or “1”. The next variable (41) is the total/sum score. The last 8 variables (42-49) are demographic variables including gender, plans to major in the life sciences, class level/year in college, ethnicity, minority membership, English as the student’s first language, course type, and type of institution. A complete description of this dataset can be found in the documentation for the {ShinyItemAnalysis} package and additional information can also be found in the validation study for the HCI.

1.1) Dataset Preparation and Preliminary Inspection
The first step is to load the {ShinyItemAnalysis} package and the HCIdata dataset into RStudio. Next, subsets of variables from the dataset are extracted into new objects to make it easier to refer to them in subsequent analyses.

## Load the package and dataset
library(ShinyItemAnalysis)
data("HCIdata")

## Extract variables to facilitate analysis
items_unscored <- HCIdata[ , 1:20]
items_scored <- HCIdata[ ,21:40]

Before performing any analyses, a preliminary inspection of the total score distribution provides a useful overview of the instrument’s performance and suitability for subsequent analyses. This can be done by examining a histogram and descriptive statistics of the total scores. The {psych} package includes the describe() function which provides useful descriptive statistics, as well as other useful functions which will be used elsewhere in this project. Some key issues to look for include: excessive skewness (which indicates a floor or ceiling effect), multimodality (which may indicate multidimensionality or distinct subgroups in the sample), and insufficient variability in scores (which can attenuate or destabilize estimates due to restriction of range).

## Load the {psych} package
library(psych)

## Create a histogram and compute descriptive statistics
hist(HCIdata$total)







describe(HCIdata$total)

   vars   n  mean   sd median trimmed  mad min max range  skew kurtosis   se
X1    1 669 12.13 3.65     12   12.22 4.45   3  20    17 -0.17    -0.68 0.14


 
Key Takeaways: Overall, the total score distribution appears healthy. The mean of 12.13 indicates that the average individual scored roughly 60.7%, which suggests that the difficulty of the test is well-aligned with the target population. The skewness of -0.17 is very small and indicates no ceiling or floor effects. The kurtosis of -0.68 indicates that the distribution is slightly platykurtic (flatter peak/thinner tails), which is desirable for differentiating students across the middle range of the score distribution. Lastly, the range of 17 and the standard deviation of 3.65 suggests that there is sufficient variation in the total scores.

1.2) Classical Reliability Analysis

1.2.1) How is Internal Consistency a Measure of Reliability?
The most common form of reliability that is analyzed in practice is internal consistency, which is typically estimated and reported using Cronbach’s alpha. Internal consistency can be informally defined as the extent to which the items correlate with one another and thus appear to be measuring the same thing. This informal definition raises a natural question: how is internal consistency a measure of reliability? Internal consistency seems to be about the consistency of items within an instrument, while reliability seems to be about the consistency of scores obtained when repeated measures of the same instrument are taken. This raises a perhaps even more fundamental question: how can the reliability of an instrument be meaningful without requiring repeated measures? These questions can be answered by examining the assumptions of the classical test theory (CTT) framework. The core component of the CTT framework is the classical true score model, which is developed as follows.


1.2.2) The Classical True Score Model

1.2.2.1) The Population Concept
First, consider a population of test-takers which is indexed by the subscript p. The CTT framework relies on the concept of a population and assumes that such a population can be meaningfully defined. Under the CTT framework, the population concept is necessary because properties such as reliability are not meaningful when looking at only one individual. Rather, these properties are joint properties of the test and the population for which the test applies. The use of the population concept affords some practical benefits for the CTT framework: the model assumptions can be relatively weak and broadly applicable, and many statistics can now be estimated. Furthermore, many scenarios where CTT is appropriate involve norm-referencing and ranking individuals within a specified population, so there is some conceptual motivation for invoking the population concept. However, the reliance on the population concept, and the resulting joint properties, is not always desirable. In fact, Georg Rasch, in developing his theory of measurement, explicitly wanted to avoid the reliance on the population concept. While the CTT framework is well-suited for relative measurement, Rasch was interested in a framework capable of absolute measurement. For absolute measurement, the difficulty of an item should not depend on the specific persons used to calibrate it, and the ability of a person should not depend on the specific items used to measure it. This is the principle of specific objectivity which the Rasch model is built around. In other words, if the Rasch model holds, these properties are no longer joint properties; they truly belong to either the test or the individual.


1.2.2.2) The Propensity Distribution
Next, each individual in the population is assumed to have a true score T_p, which is defined as the expectation of a hypothetical propensity distribution for that individual p, in which the hypothetical replications in the propensity distribution are indexed by h. Note that the expectation operator has the subscript h, which means that we are averaging over the propensity distribution of a specific individual. When the expectation operator has the subscript p (i.e., E_p[\,]), this means that we are averaging over the population of individuals. This will help us keep track of within-person versus between-person variability. Additionally, note that for each individual p, T_p is a constant, since that individual’s propensity distribution has been collapsed into a single value.
 T_p \equiv E_h[X_p]
To understand this definition of true score and where it comes from, let us examine the canonical thought experiment which is often used to motivate it, as well as the propensity interpretation of probability. The canonical thought experiment comes from Lazarsfeld (1959), which is restated in Lord & Novick (1968), and involves a certain fellow named Mr. Brown:

“Suppose we ask an individual, Mr. Brown, repeatedly whether he is in favor of the United Nations; suppose further that after each question we ‘wash his brains’ and ask him the same question again. Because Mr. Brown is not certain as to how he feels about the United Nations, he will sometimes give a favorable and sometimes an unfavorable answer. Having gone through this procedure many times, we then compute the proportion of times Mr. Brown was in favor of the United Nations…There is one interesting consequence of this version of the probability notion. A specific Mr. Brown, for instance, might feel that it is his duty to be in favor of the United Nations. Therefore, if he is asked a question when he is sober, his probability–or, if you please, his propensity–to be in favor of the United Nations might be rather high. Under the influence of alcohol, however, his hostility to the international organization might come out. Therefore, his probability under the influence of alcohol could be different than his probability if he were sober…Thus, we have a concept of probability which can apply to a single individual; furthermore, this probability or propensity itself can be different under various conditions.” (Lord & Novick, 1968, p. 29-30)

The idea of the propensity distribution comes from the propensity interpretation of probability, which is often attributed to Karl Popper. Popper originally developed the propensity interpretation within the context of quantum physics, in which certain measurements cannot be repeated exactly. Rather than interpreting the probability of an event as the long-run frequency of that event in an infinite series of independent replications, as in the frequentist interpretation, the propensity interpretation assumes that each random experiment has a disposition to behave in a certain way, based on the specific conditions of the system and its environment. The propensity interpretation draws from a long tradition of research in philosophy into dispositions, which are also called powers, and are closely related to the idea of laws of nature. An example of a disposition which is often used for illustrative purposes is fragility: fragile objects, due to their internal structure (properties of the system) are disposed to break when the right kind of force is applied to them (environmental conditions). Furthermore, an object can possess a disposition even if the disposition is never realized; i.e. an object can be fragile even if it is never actually broken.
The propensity interpretation is not without issues; as Denny Borsboom says, there are no unproblematic interpretations. However, the propensity interpretation was clearly very influential in psychometrics around the time of Lord & Novick, and it maps surprisingly well to issues in latent construct measurement, where the conditions required for the frequentist interpretation to work well do not typically hold. The important takeaway for test theory is that, while an infinite number of independent test administrations is not possible in practice, we nevertheless assume that each individual does by nature possess a disposition to score in a certain way. This disposition is represented by a hypothetical distribution with a certain finite mean and variance.
From the definition of true score, it follows that each observed score X_p is randomly drawn from an individual’s propensity distribution, and that the observed score differs from that individual’s true score T_p by some random value e_p, which is called the individual’s error score. This decomposition of observed score is true by definition.
X_p \equiv T_p + e_p 
Or equivalently:
 e_p \equiv X_p - T_p 
It also follows that the error score has a mean of zero for each individual:
 E_h[e_p] = 0 
Since:
 E_h[e_p] = E_h[X_p - T_p]   = E_h[X_p] - E_h[T_p]   = T_p - T_p   =0 
Thus far, we have been considering within-person variability by considering an individual’s propensity distribution. Now, we will consider between-person variability in the population of individuals so that we can meaningfully talk about the variances and covariances involving the true and error scores. Since we will now deal with between-person variability, we will use the population level expectation operator E_p[\,], which means that we are averaging over the population of individuals. Similarly, we will use the population level variance Var_p[\,] and covariance Cov_p[\,] operators (which can be defined using the population level expectation operator) to indicate that we are referring to the variance and covariance between different individuals.
It turns out that the variance in observed scores between individuals in the population can be decomposed into the sum of the variance in true scores between individuals in the population and the variance in error scores between individuals in the population:
 Var_p[X_p] = Var_p[T_p] + Var_p[e_p] 
This is because:
Var_p[X_p] = Var_p[T_p + e_p]  = Var_p[T_p] + Var_p[e_p] + 2Cov_p[T_p, e_p] 
It can be shown that:
 Cov_p[T_p, e_p] = 0
Since:
 Cov_p[T_p, e_p] = E_p[T_p \cdot e_p] - E_p[T_p] \cdot E_p[e_p]
The second term vanishes, since:
 E_p[e_p] = E_p[E_h[e_p]]  = E_p[0]  =0 
Thus:
 Cov_p[T_p, e_p] = E_p[T_p \cdot e_p]   = E_p[E_h[T_p \cdot e_p]]   = E_p[T_p \cdot E_h[e_p]]   = E_p[T_p \cdot 0]   = E_p[0]   =0 
Using the population level variance decomposition result above, the reliability coefficient can be conceptually defined as the proportion of variance in observed scores which can be attributed to the variance in true scores.
 Rel_p[X_p] \equiv \frac{Var_p[T_p]}{Var_p[X_p]} = \frac{Var_p[T_p]}{Var_p[T_p]+Var_p[e_p]} 



1.2.3) The Additional Assumptions
The propensity definition of the true score and the conceptual definition of reliability are the two basic definitions of the classical true score model. However, in its current form, the classical true score model is very limited in its utility. The issue is that the model only explains a single measurement at a time for each individual, which is typically the total/sum score for the test.
This is a problem because there is, in fact, no way to estimate reliability under the classical true score model as defined thus far. The model is unidentified, since there are more unknowns (T_p and e_p) than there are observed values (X_p). This issue can be resolved by modeling multiple measurements from each individual in the form of item scores. With multiple items, with the items in the test being indexed by i (when multiple items are being referred to at once, they will be indexed with j and k), the CTT model becomes:
 T_{pi} \equiv E_h[X_{pi}]   X_{pi} \equiv T_{pi} + e_{pi} 
However, modeling multiple items for each individual does not, by itself, solve the issue of model identification. This is because, without further assumptions about the items, increasing the number of items only increases the number of equations in the system without actually increasing the ratio of observed quantities to unknown quantities. There are still more unknowns (T_{pi} and e_{pi}) than knowns (X_{pi}). Thus, additional assumptions are needed in order for the information from the items to be utilized.
First, the assumption of local independence is almost always made. This assumption states that, given the vector of item true scores for an individual, the item observed scores for that individual are conditionally independent. In other words, the vector of item true scores for an individual is the only thing that determines how that individual will respond to the items. This is sometimes called the strong form of local independence. Formally, the assumption is stated as follows:
 X_{pj} \perp X_{pk} \; | \; (T_{p1},...,T_{pk}), \; \text{for all items} \; j \neq k
This assumption provides the following useful result, which is that no two distinct item error scores covary for the same individual. Note that the subscript of the covariance operator indicates that the result refers to the within-person covariance between the propensity distributions for distinct items.
Cov_h[e_{pj},e_{pk}]=0, \; \text{for items} \; j \neq k
Using the within-person result, it can be shown that the result also holds at the population level:
Cov_p[e_{pj}, e_{pk}] = 0, \; \text{for items} \; j \neq k
Since:
Cov_p[e_{pj}, e_{pk}] = E_p[e_{pj} \cdot e_{pk}] - E_p[e_{pj}] \cdot E_p[e_{pk}]
The second term vanishes, since:
E_p[e_{pi}] = 0
Thus:
Cov_p[e_{pj}, e_{pk}] = E_p[e_{pj} \cdot e_{pk}] = E_p[E_h[e_{pj} \cdot e_{pk}]] = E_p[Cov_h[e_{pj}, e_{pk}] + E_h[e_{pj}] \cdot E_h[e_{pk}]] = E_p[0 + 0\cdot0] =0
The population level result will be useful later in deriving the variance decomposition of the total scores.
Next, there are additional assumptions made about (1) how the true scores between items relate to each other, and (2) how the error variances between items relate to each other. Here, there are four sets of additional assumptions which are nested within each other: parallel, tau-equivalent, essentially tau-equivalent, and congeneric items.
The assumption of parallel items states that all items have the same true score T_p and the same error variance \sigma^2_{e_p} within the same individual. The assumption of parallel measurements is the strictest because it implies that all items within an individual are fully interchangeable. Statistically, there is no way to tell the items apart. Under these conditions, the CTT model becomes:
X_{pi}=T_p+e_{pi}, \; \text{where} \; Var_h[e_{pi}]=\sigma^2_{e_p} \; \text{for all items} \; i
The assumption of tau-equivalent measurements is slightly weaker by allowing the error variance to differ between items within the same individual. The CTT model becomes:
X_{pi}=T_p+e_{pi}, \; \text{where} \; Var_h[e_{pi}] \; \text{can differ across items} \; i
The assumption of essentially tau-equivalent measurements is weaker still by allowing the true scores to differ from a common true score T_p by some additive constant a_i between items within the same individual. The CTT model becomes:
X_{pi}=a_i+T_p+e_{pi}, \; \text{where} \; Var_h[e_{pi}] \; \text{can differ across items} \; i
Lastly, the assumption of congeneric measurements is the weakest by allowing the true scores to differ from a common true score T_p by some linear transformation of T_p within each individual. The CTT model becomes:
X_{pi}=a_i+\lambda_iT_p+e_{pi}, \; \text{where} \; Var_h[e_{pi}] \; \text{can differ across items} \; i
It can be shown that under the conditions of essential tau-equivalence or stricter, Cronbach’s alpha is equivalent to the reliability of the total scores in the population defined conceptually as the proportion of variance in observed total scores in the population which is attributable to the variance in true scores in the population. Additionally, it can be shown that under the weaker conditions of congeneric measurements, Cronbach’s alpha is a lower bound for reliability.
To see why this is the case, first let’s define the total score X_p for each individual p as the sum of their item observed scores:
 X_p \equiv \sum_{i} X_{pi} 
Next, under essential tau-equivalence, the total score X_p is equal to:
X_p = \sum_{i}(a_i+T_p+e_{pi})  = \sum_ia_i + \sum_iT_p + \sum_ie_{pi}  = A + kT_p + E_p 
Where:
 A \equiv \sum_{i}a_i  E_p \equiv \sum_{i} e_{pi} 
Next, the total score variance between individuals in the population can be decomposed as follows:
 Var_p[X_p] = Var_p[A + kT_p + E_p]  = Var_p[A] + Var_p[kT_p] + Var_p[E_p] + 2Cov_p[A, kT_p] + 2Cov_p[A, E_p] + 2Cov[kT_p,E_p] 
Since A is a constant, all of the variance and covariance terms containing A are equal to zero. Thus,
Var_p[X_p] = Var_p[kT_p] + Var_p[E_p] + 2Cov[kT_p,E_p] = k^2Var_p[T_p] + Var_p[E_p] + 2kCov_p[T_p,E_p] =k^2Var_p[T_p] + Var_p[E_p] + 2kCov_p[T_p, \sum_{i}e_{pi}] =k^2Var_p[T_p] + Var_p[E_p] + 2k\sum_{i}Cov_p[T_p,e_{pi}]
It can be shown that:
Cov_p[T_p,e_{pi}]=0
Since:
Cov_p[T_p,e_{pi}] = E_p[T_p \cdot e_{pi}] - E_p[T_p] \cdot E_p[e_{pi}] = E_p[T_p \cdot e_{pi}] - E_p[T_p] \cdot 0 = E_p[T_p \cdot e_{pi}] = E_p[E_h[T_p \cdot e_{pi}]] = E_p[T_p \cdot E_h[e_{pi}]] = E_p[T \cdot 0] = E_p[0] =0
Thus, the variance of the total scores becomes:
Var_p[X_p] = k^2Var_p[T_p] + Var_p[E_p] + 2k\sum_{i}0 = k^2Var_p[T_p] + Var_p[E_p] = k^2Var_p[T_p] + Var_p[\sum_{i}e_{pi}] = k^2Var_p[T_p] + \sum_{i}Var_p[e_{pi}] + 2\sum_{j<k}Cov_p[e_{pj},e_{pk}]
By the local independence assumption, the covariance terms are equal to zero. Thus the variance of the total scores is:
Var_p[X_p] = k^2Var_p[T_p] + \sum_{i}Var_p[e_{pi}]
The reliability of the total scores X_p in the population of test-takers p can now be defined conceptually as the proportion of variance in total scores which is attributable to the true scores (the term containing T_p).
Rel_p[X_p] \equiv \frac{k^2Var_p[T_p]}{k^2Var_p[T_p] + \sum_{i}Var_p[e_{pi}]}
This formula can be transformed into the familiar formula for Cronbach’s alpha by restating the unobserved quantities (Var_p[T_p] and \sum_{i}Var_p[e_{pi}]) in terms of the observed quantities (Var_p[X_p] and Var_p[X_{pi}]). It can be shown that:
Var_p[T_p] = \frac{Var_p[X_p]-\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]}{k(k-1)} \sum_{i}Var_p[e_{pi}] = \frac{k\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]-Var_p[X_p]}{k-1}
The result for Var_p[T_p] can be obtained by considering the equation for the total score variance decomposition as well as the equation for the per-item variance decomposition. These form a system of two equations. First, let’s derive the per-item variance decomposition. Under essential tau equivalence:
Var_p[X_{pi}] = Var_p[a_i+T_p+e_{pi}] = Var_p[a_i] + Var_p[T_p] + Var_p[e_{pi}] + 2Cov_p[a_i,T_p] + 2Cov_p[a_i,e_{pi}] + 2Cov_p[T_p,e_{pi}]
Since a_i is a constant, all of the variance and covariance terms involving a_i are equal to zero. Additionally, the population-level covariance between the true and error scores is equal to zero. Thus,
Var_p[X_{pi}] = Var_p[T_p] + Var_p[e_{pi}] Summing across all k items:
\Rightarrow \sum_iVar_p[X_{pi}] = \sum_i(Var_p[T_p]+Var_p[e_{pi}]) = \sum_iVar_p[T_p] + \sum_iVar_p[e_{pi}] = kVar_p[T_p] + \sum_iVar_p[e_{pi}]
Now we can consider the system of two equations:
Var_p[X_p] = k^2Var_p[T_p] + \sum_iVar_p[e_{pi}] \sum_iVar_p[X_{pi}] = kVar_p[T_p] + \sum_iVar_p[e_{pi}]
Next, subtract the second equation from the first. The summed error variance terms cancel out, resulting in:
Var_p[X_p] - \sum_iVar_p[X_{pi}] = k^2Var_p[T_p] - kVar_p[T_p] = (k^2-k)Var_p[T_p] = k(k-1)Var_p[T_p]
Dividing the lefthand side by k(k-1), we have shown that the unobserved term Var_p[T_p] can be written in terms of the observed terms:
Var_p[T_p] = \frac{Var_p[X_p] - \sum_iVar_p[X_{pi}]}{k(k-1)}
Now we will consider the second unobserved term \sum_iVar_p[e_{pi}]. Starting with the second equation in the system of two equations:
\sum_iVar_p[X_{pi}] = kVar_p[T_p] + \sum_iVar_p[e_{pi}]
Rearrange:
\sum_iVar_p[E_{pi}] = \sum_iVar_p[X_{pi}] - kVar_p[T_p]
Substituting the previous result for Var_p[T_p]:
\sum_iVar_p[E_{pi}] = \sum_iVar_p[X_{pi}] - k \cdot \frac{Var_p[X_p] - \sum_iVar_p[X_{pi}]}{k(k-1)} = \sum_iVar_p[X_{pi}] - \frac{Var_p[X_p] - \sum_iVar_p[X_{pi}]}{k-1} = \frac{(k-1)\sum_iVar_p[X_{pi}] - Var_p[X_p] + \sum_iVar_p[X_{pi}]}{k-1} = \frac{k\sum_iVar_p[X_{pi}] - Var_p[X_p]}{k-1}
Thus, the second unobserved term can also be written in terms of the observed terms. Now that we have restated both of the unobserved terms, we can substitute them into the formula for the reliability coefficient and simplify:
Rel_p[X_p] = \frac{k^2Var_p[T_p]}{k^2Var_p[T_p] + \sum_{i}Var_p[e_{pi}]} = \frac{k^2 \cdot \frac{Var_p[X_p]-\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]}{k(k-1)}}{k^2 \cdot \frac{Var_p[X_p]-\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]}{k(k-1)} + \frac{k\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]-Var_p[X_p]}{k-1}}  = \frac{\frac{k(Var_p[X_p]-\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}])}{k-1}}{\frac{k(Var_p[X_p]-\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}])}{k-1}+\frac{k\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]-Var_p[X_p]}{k-1}} = \frac{\frac{kVar_p[X_p]-k\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]}{k-1}}{\frac{kVar_p[X_p]-k\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]}{k-1}+\frac{k\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]-Var_p[X_p]}{k-1}} =\frac{\frac{kVar_p[X_p]-k\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]}{k-1}}{\frac{kVar_p[X_p]-Var_p[X_p]+k\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]-k\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]}{k-1}} =\frac{\frac{kVar_p[X_p]-k\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]}{k-1}}{\frac{(k-1)Var_p[X_p]}{k-1}} =\frac{\frac{kVar_p[X_p]-k\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]}{k-1}}{Var_p[X_p]} =\frac{kVar_p[X_p]-k\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]}{(k-1)Var_p[X_p]} =\frac{k(Var_p[X_p]-\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}])}{(k-1)Var_p[X_p]} =\frac{k}{k-1} \cdot \frac{Var_p[X_p]-\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]}{Var_p[X_p]} =\frac{k}{k-1}(1-\frac{\sum_{i}Var_p[X_{pi}]}{Var_p[X_p]}) = \alpha
Thus, we have shown that under the assumptions of essential tau-equivalence, the definition of the reliability of the total scores in the population, as the proportion of observed score variance which is attributable to true score variance, is equivalent to Cronbach’s alpha. The proof that Cronbach’s alpha is a lower bound for reliability under the assumptions of congeneric items is a bit more complicated, so it is not included here, but can be found in Appendix A.
To conclude the brief theoretical exposition, we see that the CTT framework makes additional assumptions beyond the classical true score model which makes it so that multiple item scores on one test can be used to estimate the reliability of measurement without requiring multiple administrations of the same test to the same individual.
The tradeoff for this nice theoretical result is that the assumptions of either essential tau-equivalence or congeneric measurements have to be tenable. If we claim that the measurements are essentially tau-equivalent, then we are saying that all items load equally on the underlying construct (analogous to equal discrimination). If this is unreasonable, then we may need to settle for congeneric measurements, in which case Cronbach’s alpha only provides a lower bound for reliability.
Another important assumption underlying the use of Cronbach’s alpha is that the variables are continuous. When the variables are dichotomous, the Pearson correlations used to calculate Cronbach’s alpha are known to underestimate the true relationship between items which have different difficulty levels. Consequently, the estimate of Cronbach’s alpha is attenuated.
For the HCI, the item responses are hypothesized to reflect an underlying continuous variable (understanding of homeostasis), but the item responses have had an artificial structure imposed on them via dichotomous scoring. Thus, the assumption of continuous variables is violated, and Cronbach’s alpha likely underestimates the true internal consistency of the instrument. The ordinal alpha based on tetrachoric correlations may be more appropriate here.
Unlike the Pearson correlation, the tetrachoric correlation is not computed from the paired values directly. Rather, the tetrachoric correlation assumes that there is a normally distributed latent variable underlying each item. For each pair of items, the tetrachoric correlation is estimated from the observed 2×2 frequency table using the method of maximum likelihood. Thus, the tetrachoric correlation is itself a model which depends on assumptions.
It is useful to report both the coefficient alpha and the ordinal alpha for two reasons. The first reason is the difference in interpretation. The coefficient alpha is an estimate of the reliability of the total scores and reflects the reliability of the instrument as it is operationally scored and used. The ordinal alpha is an estimate of the reliability of the underlying continuous variables, which reflects the theoretical reliability of the instrument if the underlying attribute is normally distributed and could be measured without information loss from the items being dichotomously scored. The second reason for reporting both estimates is that the difference between the estimates itself provides useful diagnostic information. If the ordinal alpha is not much higher than the coefficient alpha, then this suggests that there is little information loss from dichotomous scoring. Conversely, a substantial gap suggests that meaningful information is lost by dichotomous scoring.


1.2.4) Application of Theory to the HCI
Cronbach’s alpha can be calculated using the alpha() function in the {psych} package. The ordinal alpha can be calculated by first calculating the tetrachoric correlations between the scored items using the tetrachoric() function in the {psych} package and then using the resulting tetrachoric correlation matrix ($rho) as the input to the alpha() function.

### Coefficient alpha using Pearson correlations
psych::alpha(items_scored)$feldt


   95% confidence boundaries (Feldt)
 lower alpha upper
  0.68  0.72  0.75

### Ordinal alpha using tetrachoric correlations
tetra <- tetrachoric(items_scored)
psych::alpha(tetra$rho)$feldt


   95% confidence boundaries (Feldt)
 lower alpha upper
   0.7  0.83  0.92


The Cronbach’s alpha estimate is .72 (95% CI [.68, .75]) and the ordinal alpha estimate is .83 (95% CI [.70, .92]). The point estimates differ by .11, which is consistent with some degree of information loss from dichotomous scoring; however, since the confidence intervals overlap, the data alone cannot determine if the two alpha estimates are significantly different. Additionally, the width of the confidence interval for the ordinal alpha estimate (width = .22) is around three times larger than for the coefficient alpha estimate (width = .07), which is consistent with the additional uncertainty introduced by the maximum likelihood estimation of the tetrachoric correlations.
The internal consistency of the composite scores is not particularly strong for an instrument which attempts to measure a single construct. According to a frequently cited guideline by Nunnally (1978), a Cronbach’s alpha of .70 or above is acceptable for early stages of research. However, for applied research, a Cronbach’s alpha of .90 or higher is typically recommended (Lance et al., 2006).
The Spearman-Brown prophecy formula can be used to predict the reliability of the instrument if the number of items were to be increased. Note that the Spearman-Brown prophecy formula assumes that the items are parallel. The formula is less accurate for essentially tau-equivalent items and even less accurate for congeneric items, so the results should not be interpreted too seriously. The spearman.brown() function in the {CTT} package can be used to perform calculations using the Spearman-Brown prophecy formula.

## Load the {CTT} package
library(CTT)

## Predicted factor of test length increase required for Cronbach's alpha = .90
spearman.brown(.72, .90, n.or.r = "r")

$n.new
[1] 3.5

## Predicted factor of test length increase required for ordinal alpha = .90
spearman.brown(.83, .90, n.or.r = "r")

$n.new
[1] 1.843373


 
Key Takeaways: The Cronbach’s alpha estimate is .72 (95% CI [.68, .75]) and the ordinal alpha estimate is .83 (95% CI [.70, .92]). The estimated reliability of the total scores for the population is not particularly strong for an instrument which attempts to measure a single construct. According to a frequently cited guideline by Nunnally (1978), a Cronbach’s alpha of .70 or above is acceptable for early stages of research. However, for applied research, a Cronbach’s alpha of .90 or higher is typically recommended (Lance et al., 2006). The Spearman-Brown prophecy formula predicts that a Cronbach’s alpha of .90 would be achieved with 70 items and an ordinal alpha of .90 would be achieved with 37 items.

1.3) Classical Item Analysis
Classical item analysis involves examining each item’s difficulty, discrimination, and impact on test reliability. For dichotomous items, the item difficulty is simply the proportion of individuals who correctly answered the item, which is referred to as the p-value. The item discrimination can be examined by taking the point-biserial correlation between the item and the total scores, which is called the item-total correlation. The point-biserial correlation is equivalent to the Pearson correlation between a dichotomous variable and a continuous variable. An issue worth noting here is that, since the total scores contain the item which is being analyzed, the point-biserial correlation between the two variables will always be inflated since the item is partly correlated with itself. Thus, it’s helpful to look at the item-rest correlation, which is the point-biserial correlation between the item and the total scores with that item removed. Lastly, the impact of an item on test reliability can be examined by calculating the Cronbach’s alpha with that item removed, which is called the alpha-if-deleted or alpha-if-dropped.
These item statistics are considered “classical” because (1) they can be calculated from the sample moments alone (means, variances, and covariances of the data), and (2) they are not parameters within a generative probability model which specifies a joint distribution over the variables involved, such as in item response theory models.
The p-value is a proportion which ranges from 0 to 1. For educational assessment, it is often desirable to have slightly easier items with a difficulty around p = .60, meaning that around 60% of individuals correctly answered the item. This is because challenging items can result in frustration for the test-takers, especially if there are a large number of them and the test-taker is repeatedly struggling to answer them. However, challenging items are not necessarily problematic and may be important to include for content coverage reasons. On the other hand, extreme difficulty values are problematic because the variance of a dichotomous variable shrinks as the p-value deviates from p = .50, and this limits the possible values of the point-biserial correlation. A reasonable range is that item difficulties should be between p = .10 and p = .90.
The item-total and item-rest correlations are correlation coefficients which can range from -1 to 1. We will focus on the item-rest correlation, since it is generally preferred as it provides a less biased measure of item discrimination. A common guideline is that an item-rest correlation above .40 is excellent, between .30 and .39 is good, between .20 and .29 is acceptable, and below .20 is poor. Additionally, negative item-rest correlations are highly problematic, since they indicate that individuals who got the item correct were less likely to get the other items correct. This is the opposite of what should be the case if the items measure the same construct.
The alpha-if-deleted statistic is the Cronbach’s alpha of the instrument with the item removed and has the same range and interpretation as Cronbach’s alpha. Items which contribute positively to reliability should have an alpha-if-deleted which is less than the overall alpha, since removing that item would weaken the internal consistency of the instrument. Items with an alpha-if-deleted which is greater than the overall alpha should be flagged for review, since this indicates that the instrument is more internally consistent without that item. A higher alpha-if-deleted is especially indicative for tests with a small number of items, since Cronbach’s alpha is partly a function of the number of items. For a test with a small number of items, a higher alpha-if-deleted indicates that the internal consistency of the test would still be higher without that item, despite the decrease in test length.

1.4) Classical Distractor Analysis
Before performing distractor analysis, there is a minor issue with the HCIdata dataset that needs to be corrected. Item 5 (A5) should have four response options (A/B/C/D). However, looking at the dataset, two entries have been incorrectly coded as lowercase “c” rather than uppercase “C”, resulting in the variable having 5 factor levels (A/B/C/c/D). This can be easily corrected using the fct_recode() function in the {forcats} package, which is part of the tidyverse family of R packages.

## Load the forcats package
library(forcats)

## Correct the data entry issue for item 5
items_unscored$A5 <- fct_recode(items_unscored$A5, "C" = "c")

Now the two factor levels have been merged. Looking at the dataset, item A5 now has 4 factor levels (A/B/C/D), which is correct. Note that not all items have 4 factor levels; the majority have either 3 or 4 factor levels, with a few items having 5 factor levels. There are no additional issues with the dataset, so we may proceed with distractor analysis.
Distractor analysis may be divided into “classical” and “model-based” approaches. This section covers classical distractor analysis, while a later section will cover model-based approaches such as the nominal response model (NRM). Classical distractor analysis primarily involves examining statistics such as the proportions of test-takers who select each distractor and the point-biserial or biserial correlations between each distractor and the total scores. The primary goal of classical distractor analysis is to guide item development by identifying non-functioning or non-discriminating distractors.
Non-functioning distractors are distractors which are selected by a very low percentage of test-takers. A common rule-of-thumb is that distractors which are selected by less than 5% of test-takers are non-functioning. However, an exception to this rule can be made for very easy items. For instance, for a multiple-choice item in which 85% of test-takers chose the correct answer, it is likely that many of the distractors would be considered non-functioning under the 5% rule. However, such distractors are not necessarily problematic, and such items can still have good discrimination and be useful for content coverage purposes.
Non-discriminating distractors are distractors which are equally likely to be selected across the total score range. Good distractors test for misconceptions which are more common in test-takers with a lower total score. As total score increases, test-takers are expected to not have as many misconceptions, and thus should be less likely to select the distractors. If a distractor is roughly equally likely to be selected by all test-takers, no matter their total score, then this suggests that the functioning of the distractor may be unrelated to the construct of interest. For instance, the distractor may be selected due to confusing language or an unintentional cue in the item stem. Typically, the non-discriminating distractors of interest are those which are not also non-functioning, otherwise they would be simply considered non-functioning distractors.
An efficient way to screen for non-functioning and non-discriminating distractors is to examine trace plots, which are also called distractor plots. Distractor plots can be created using the plotDistractorAnalysis() function in the {ShinyDataAnalysis} package. To make the plots look a little nicer, the {ggplot2} and {patchwork} packages are also used.

## Load packages
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

## Create the distractor plots for all 20 items
distractor_plots <- plotDistractorAnalysis(
                        Data = items_unscored, 
                        key = HCIkey, 
                        num.groups = 4, 
                        item = "all")

## Make all plots have the same color scheme for response options
## Also make all plots have more tick marks on the vertical axis
for (i in seq_along(distractor_plots)) {
  distractor_plots[[i]] <- distractor_plots[[i]] + 
    scale_color_manual(values = c(A = "red",
                                  B = "green",
                                  C = "cyan",
                                  D = "blue",
                                  E = "magenta")) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1),
                       limits = c(0, 1))
                                        }

To understand the elements of a distractor plot, let us examine the distractor plot for item 1 below. The horizontal axis represents the total score, which has been grouped into 4 quantiles. Group 1 includes the lowest 25% of total scores, group 2 includes the next 25%, and so on. The vertical axis represents the proportion of test-takers who selected each response option. The correct answer, as defined by the scoring key (HCIkey), is shown using a solid line, while distractors are shown using dashed lines.

## Examine distractor plot for item 1
distractor_plots$A1








Now let’s examine the distractor plots for all 20 items. The plots are neatly summarized into a single multi-panel figure. The legends and axis titles are omitted for visual clarity, and all plots within the figure use the same coloring scheme described in the code above.

## Combine all plots into a multi-panel figure
wrap_plots(distractor_plots, ncol = 4) & 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 7),
        axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 5),
        legend.position = "none")








Numerical values for the selection proportions, as well as additional statistics such as the sample size for each response option and the point-biserial correlations between each response option and the total scores, are a useful supplement to the distractor plots. The DistractorAnalysis() function in the {ShinyItemAnalysis} package will provide the selection proportions by group, but it does not provide the additional statistics. Thus, I prefer the {CTT} package which has a very similar function called distractorAnalysis(). In fact, the function in the {ShinyItemAnalysis} package is a modified version of the function in the {CTT} package, so the underlying code is very similar.

Now that the distractor plots and statistics for all 20 items are computed, let us examine the items for any issues with distractor functioning. First, an examination of the distractor plots provides a useful overall picture of distractor functioning. Here are some useful guidelines when examining distractor plots:

The correct option (solid line) should trend upwards.
The distractors (dashed lines) should trend downwards.
The highest total score group should not have any distractors which are selected more frequently than the correct option.
Flat trendlines suggest non-discriminating distractors.
Very low proportion trendlines suggest non-functioning distractors.
Distractors with a hill-shaped line represent a partial misconception and are inconclusive under classical methods.

An example of an easy item with a well-functioning distractors is item 3 (p = .848, r_{IR} = .344). The correct option trends upwards, the distractors trend downwards, and the distractors are selected at a substantial proportion among lower total score groups.

## Examine distractor plot for item 3
distractor_plots$A3








An example of a difficult item with well-functioning distractors is item 6 (p = .359, r_{IR} = .345). The correct option trends upwards, the distractors trend downwards, and the distractors are selected at a substantial proportion among lower total score groups. Since this item is quite difficult, we see that lower total score groups are much more likely to select the distractor option B, and that option B retains a substantial proportion even at higher total score groups.

## Examine distractor plot for item 6
distractor_plots$A6








An example of a non-functioning distractor can be found in item 12 (p = .577, r_{IR} = .300). We see that option B (green) is almost never selected, even in the lowest total score group. The selection proportions for option B according to the table above are (.03, .01, .01, .01) for the 4 groups, from lowest to highest total score.

## Examine distractor plot for item 12
distractor_plots$A12








There are no good examples of distractors which are non-discriminating across the entire total score range, which would appear as a relatively flat line across the entire plot. The closest example can be found in item 4 (p = .399, r_{IR} = .177). We see that option C (r_{IR} = -.28, shown in cyan) has a trendline which is relatively flat for the lower three total score groups, before dropping substantially for the highest total score group. This suggests that option C only really discriminates between the lower three groups and the highest group, and does not discriminate within the lower three groups themselves.

## Examine distractor plot for item 4
distractor_plots$A4








An example of a hill-shaped distractor can be found in item 17 (p = .291, r_{IR} = .049). We see that option A (r_{IR} = -.08, shown in red) has a distinctive hill-shaped trendline, which suggests that this distractor is of a different type compared to those which trend downwards monotonically; rather than affecting lower ability individuals the most, individuals need to be at a certain ability level to possess the partial understanding required for this distractor to function. Hill-shaped distractors are not necessarily problematic and could be useful and informative. However, the functioning of these distractors is inconclusive under classical distractor analyses. More sophisticated methods, such as item response theory (IRT) approaches using the nominal response model (NRM), may better explain the functioning of these distractors.

## Examine distractor plot for item 17
distractor_plots$A17








Overall, the classical distractor analysis indicates that there are relatively few problematic distractors, which makes sense as the instrument was developed with distractor functioning as a priority. There are a few potentially non-functional distractors, but there are no distractors which are non-discriminating across the entire total score range. Based on overall selection proportions, the potential non-functioning distractors include:

Item 1: distractor A (prop = .04).
Item 4: distractors A (prop = .03) and B (prop = .03).
Item 9: distractor C (prop = .02).
Item 12: distractors B (prop = .02) and C (prop = .04).
Item 20: distractor A (prop = .02).

Earlier it was mentioned that a low overall selection proportion does not necessarily mean that the distractor is problematic. This is because the item may be an easy item, in which case low overall selection proportions are expected. Additionally, the distractor may be selected to a substantial degree by lower total score groups, but almost never selected by higher total score groups, resulting in a low overall selection proportion. Such distractors may still discriminate well, as indicated by the point-biserial correlations, even though they have a low overall selection proportion. Let us examine the potential non-functioning distractors with these considerations in mind.
For item 1, Distractor A has a moderate-sized negative point-biserial correlation (r_{IR} = -.25) with selection proportions (.09, .05, .01, .00) in order from lowest to highest total score group. Since option A discriminates fairly well and is selected at a substantial frequency by lower total score groups, this distractor is likely unproblematic and does not require revision.
For item 4, distractors A and B have moderately-sized negative point-biserial correlations (r_{IR} = -.27 and r_{IR} =-.26, respectively), but they are only selected at a substantial frequency by the lowest total score group, and are almost never selected by the other 3 groups, with selection proportions (.07, .01, .00, .00) and (.08, .01, .01, .00), respectively. This suggests that distractors A and B are primarily selected due to chance guessing at very low ability levels. Additionally, distractor C clearly dominates the response options, with selection proportions (.61, .60, .60, .33). The distractor functioning indicates that this item is essentially dichotomous, and is consistent with the context found in the item stem, which essentially asks whether a homeostatic control mechanism is always functioning (option D) or if it only activates in certain scenarios (option C).
For item 9, distractor C has a moderately-sized negative point-biserial correlation (r_{IR}=-.23) but is essentially only selected by the lowest total score group, with selection proportions (.06, .00, .00, .00). This suggests that distractor C is primarily selected due to chance guessing at very low ability levels and may require revision.
For item 12, distractor B has a weak negative point-biserial correlation (r_{IR}=-.14) and is essentially only selected by the lowest total score group, with selection proportions (.03, .01, .01, .01), and distractor C has a moderately-sized negative point-biserial correlation (r_{IR}=-.21) and is selected at a substantial frequency in the lower total score groups, with selection proportions (.07, .06, .03, .00). This suggests that distractor B may require revision, but distractor C is likely unproblematic.
For item 20, distractor A has a weak negative point-biserial correlation (r_{IR}=-.19) and is essentially only selected by the lowest total score group, with selection proportions (.05, .01, .00, .00). This suggests that distractor A is primarily selected due to chance guessing at very low ability levels and may require revision. Additionally, this item is structurally similar to item 4, with the distractor functioning and item stem indicating that the item is essentially dichotomous.
 
Key Takeaways: The classical distractor analysis suggests that the distractors are functioning well in general. Item 9 (distractor C) and item 12 (distractor B) are infrequently selected and are essentially only selected by the group with the lowest 25% of total scores, which suggests that these distractors may benefit from revision. Additionally, the distractor functioning for item 4 and item 20 suggests that these items are essentially dichotomous, which is consistent with the context found in the item stems. These distractors may benefit from revision, or they may be retained as is, since these items still provide useful information about test-takers.

1.5) Optimal Scaling
Before moving on to item response theory (IRT) models, it’s a good idea to examine (1) whether dichotomous scoring is appropriate, and (2) the dimensionality of the dataset.
Thus far, the items have been dichotomously scored by assigning each correct option a score of 1 and each incorrect option a score of 0. However, it is likely that some information is lost by dichotomous scoring. This is because dichotomous scoring treats each incorrect option as having equal value, which is unlikely since the distractors differ in their quality, as seen in the classical distractor analysis above. Additionally, the difference in the point estimates for Cronbach’s alpha and ordinal alpha is consistent with there being some amount of information loss from dichotomous scoring. An alternative is to use optimal scaling, which describes a set of data-driven approaches that assign different scores to each response option by optimizing for some statistical criterion.
A common statistical criterion is to choose scores which maximize the sum of item correlations (the entries in the item correlation matrix). This is equivalent to maximizing the coefficient alpha of the instrument. The corAspect() function in the {aspect} package (Mair & de Leeuw, 2010) can be used to perform optimal scaling. By default, the corAspect() function optimizes for the sum of item correlations (aspect = "aspectSum") and assumes that the variables are nominal (level = "nominal").

## Load the aspect package
library(aspect)

## Optimizing for the sum of item correlations (and thus coefficient alpha)
opt_alpha <- corAspect(items_unscored, aspect = "aspectSum", level = "nominal")

Cronbach’s alpha based on the optimal scores can be calculated using the alpha() function in the {psych} package with the transformed data matrix opt_alpha$scoremat.

## Calculate Cronbach's alpha after optimal scaling
psych::alpha(opt_alpha$scoremat)$feldt


   95% confidence boundaries (Feldt)
 lower alpha upper
  0.74  0.77  0.79


The point estimate for the Cronbach’s alpha based on the optimal scores (\alpha = .77, 95% CI [.74, .79]) is .05 higher than the point estimate for the Cronbach’s alpha based dichotomous scoring (\alpha = .72, 95% CI [.68, .75]). Given that the optimal scaling procedure maximizes Cronbach’s alpha, the observed increase is relatively small and suggests that there is not much to be gained from optimal scoring. This, in turn, suggests that there is not much reliability-relevant information lost by dichotomous scoring for this particular sample.
Additionally, the total scores based on optimal scores can be computed and the relationship between the original and optimal total scores can be examined by computing the correlation and creating a scatterplot.

## Compute optimal total scores
total_scores_opt <- unname(rowSums(opt_alpha$scoremat))

## Compare optimal and dichotomous total scores
round(cor(HCIdata$total, total_scores_opt), 3)

[1] 0.948

plot(HCIdata$total, total_scores_opt)








The correlation between the original total scores and the new total scores is very high (r = .948), which indicates that there is a strong positive linear relationship between the original total scores and the new total scores. Additionally, the squared correlation (R^2 = .899) indicates that, in a simple linear regression model, around 90% of the variation in the new total scores is explained by the linear relationship with the original total scores.
 
Key Takeaways: The results of the optimal scaling procedure suggest that there is not much reliability-relevant information lost by dichotomous scoring for this particular sample. The Cronbach’s alpha based on optimal scores (\alpha = .77, 95% CI [.74, .79])) is only slightly larger than the Cronbach’s alpha based on dichotomous scores (\alpha = .72, 95% CI [.68, .75]). Additionally, there is a strong linear relationship between the original total scores and the total scores obtained using optimal scaling (r = .948, R^2 = .899).

1.6) Dimensionality Analysis
The dimensionality of the dataset can be examined by performing exploratory factor analysis on the tetrachoric correlation matrix. Before performing factor analysis, it’s helpful to examine the data to see how suitable it is. This can be done by (1) examining the correlation matrix using a heatmap, (2) the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) index, and (3) Bartlett’s test of sphericity.
First, a heatmap of the tetrachoric correlation matrix will provide an overall picture of the correlations between items and help us identify clusters of large correlations. The {corrplot} package provides many helpful tools for creating heatmaps on correlation matrices.

## Load the required package
library(corrplot)

corrplot 0.95 loaded

## Create the heatmap using the tetrachoric correlation matrix
corrplot(tetra$rho,
         method = "color",
         order = "AOE", 
         type = "lower",
         diag = FALSE)








The items have been ordered so that clusters of correlations are more visually clear using the “angular order of eigenvectors” (order = "AOE") method. From the heatmap, we see that the correlations are almost all positive and small in magnitude. Additionally, there appears to be a cluster of near zero correlations on the left. These include item 17, item 4, item 9, and item 7, which appear to not correlate with most of the other items.
Furthermore, item 4, item 9, and item 20 seem to form a cluster at the top left. Examining the stems for these items reveals that the items test the same basic principle, which is that a homeostatic mechanism is always functioning, rather than being on or off. Item 4 is a conceptual version, while item 9 and item 20 are applied versions of this principle. These three items are the only items which test this principle, so this is evidence that these items could tap into an underlying factor.
Additionally, there appears to be an especially large correlation between item 18 and item 19 (r = .593). This may suggest that there is local dependence between these items. This is a problem for factor analysis, since a pair of dependent items can be treated as a factor in solutions with a larger number of factors. Examining the item stems confirms the dependence:



Items 18 and 19 from the HCI


We see that both items involve information from sensory receptors going to control centers called integrators in homeostatic systems. The issue is that the stem for item 19 essentially states the answer for item 18. A test-taker who is unsure of how to answer item 18 can read the stem for item 19 and see that information from sensory receptors is sent to the integrators. Thus, we may want to consider omitting one of these items from the factor analysis.
Lastly, examining the stem for item 17 reveals that it requires a unique kind of reasoning which is not tested by any other items. Item 17 involves a scenario in which one of the components of the homeostatic mechanism is damaged (receptor nerves are cut so the signal does not reach the control center) and requires the test-taker to make an inference about the resulting functioning of the mechanism. This may explain the low correlations between item 17 and the rest of the items in the HCI.
Next, the information found in the tetrachoric correlation matrix can be summarized using the KMO index, which represents the proportion of variance between the variables which may be attributable to common variance.

## Calculate the KMO index using the tetrachoric correlation matrix
KMO(tetra$rho)

Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin factor adequacy

The overall MSA is 0.78, which is acceptable but not particularly strong. Kaiser (1974) provided the following guidelines: > .90 is marvelous, .80 to .90 is meritorious, .70 to .80 is average, .60 to .70 is mediocre, .50 to .60 is terrible, and < .50 is unacceptable. Based on Kaiser’s guidelines, the overall MSA is average, and is lowered by a few items with low individual MSAs: item 17 (MSA = .40), item 7 (MSA = .62), item 4 (MSA = .63), and item 9 (MSA = .63). These are the same items that appeared to not correlate with most of the other items in the heatmap.
Next, Bartlett’s test of sphericity can be used to test the hypothesis that the correlation matrix is an identity matrix. Bartlett’s test can be performed using the cortest.bartlett() function in the {psych} package.

## Perform Bartlett's test of sphericity
cortest.bartlett(tetra$rho, n = nrow(items_scored))

$chisq
[1] 3389.654

$p.value
[1] 0

Bartlett’s test is significant, which indicates that the tetrachoric correlation matrix differs significantly from an identity matrix. However, Bartlett’s test tends to always be significant as the number of variables and the sample size increases, since it becomes increasingly unlikely that every single correlation is equal to that of the identity matrix, which is what is being tested. Thus, Bartlett’s test is not particularly useful here.
The results of the preliminary analyses suggest that factor analysis can be performed, but we should not expect great results. The items will likely not factor cleanly and it will be difficult to decide which factor solutions are correct. If this is the case, we may want to consider performing factor analysis with a few problematic items omitted. The most principled items to omit are:

Item 17: unacceptable MSA (.40), item stem suggests that it requires a unique skill.
Item 19: part of dependent item pair (items 18 and 19; item 18 is retained as it has better discrimination).
Item 7: mediocre MSA (.62), item stem suggests that it requires a unique skill.

Next, the number of factors can be determined using parallel analysis. Parallel analysis compares the eigenvalues from the actual dataset against eigenvalues from simulated/resampled datasets of the same size. The idea is that a “real” factor should explain more variance than would be expected from chance alone.

## Perform parallel analysis
set.seed(1234)
fa.parallel(items_scored, fm = "ml", cor = "tet")








Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors =  7  and the number of components =  3 


Principal components analysis (PCA) analyzes total variance in each variable, so PCA eigenvalues tend to be larger and drop off faster. Factor analysis (FA) analyzes only the common variance between variables, so FA eigenvalues tend to be smaller and drop off more gradually. In this case, both results suggest that the dataset may have additional structure beyond a single construct. However, the eigenvalues also indicate that there is one dominant factor/component which is much larger than the others. This suggests that, although additional factors may explain a significant amount of variance, the dataset is essentially unidimensional.
Next, we can fit EFA models with a different number of factors to compare their model fit. Since the parallel analysis suggested 7 factors, all solutions up to 7 factors will be compared. Since EFA is being performed using tetrachoric correlations, unweighted least squares (fm = "uls") will be used instead of maximum likelihood estimation.

## Fit EFA models
fit_fa_1 <- fa(items_scored, nfactors = 1, fm = "uls", cor = "tet")
fit_fa_2 <- fa(items_scored, nfactors = 2, fm = "uls", cor = "tet")

1.8) Distractor Analysis using the Nominal Response Model
The nominal response model (NRM) (Bock, 1972) is an IRT model which is designed for unordered categorical response data. The mirt() function in the {mirt} package can be used to fit the NRM. The mirt() function takes only numeric or integer values as input. Since the unscored item responses are currently stored as factors with factor levels (e.g. “A”, “B”, “C”, …), they need to be relabeled as integers (e.g. “1”, “2”, “3”, …).

## Relabel the unscored item responses with integer labels
items_unscored_int <- data.frame(lapply(items_unscored, 
                                        function(x) as.integer(x)))

     type = "trace",

Additionally, the item and test information curves can be plotted:

## Item information curves
plot(fit_nrm, type = "infotrace",
     layout = c(4, 5),
     as.table = TRUE)









## Test information curve
plot(fit_nrm, type = "info")







## Standard error of measurement curve
plot(fit_nrm, type = "SE")








From the item information curves, we see that item 17 and item 7 appear to provide essentially no information. Additionally, item 4, item 9, and item 18 appear to be the most informative items. From the test information curves, we see that the curve peaks around \theta = -2, indicating that the instrument provides the most information for individuals with a below average ability level and provides little information for individuals with above average ability. This is consistent with the standard error of measurement curve, in which individuals with an above average ability level have a much larger SEM.
